<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines sources for two architectures (x86_64 and aarch64), both pointing to release binaries hosted on GitHub via HTTPS URLs. The sources are prebuilt tarballs from the project's own GitHub releases, which is standard practice for -bin packages. The `sha256sums` are provided and not set to 'SKIP', so the integrity of the downloaded binaries will be verified during the source fetch — this further strengthens safety.

No code is executed in the global scope or within a `pkgver()` function that would run during sourcing. The variables are simple string assignments and array definitions, with no command substitution, `eval`, or external network calls outside of the declared `source` array. The `package()` function is irrelevant here because `--noprepare` and `--nobuild` prevent it from running. Therefore, sourcing this PKGBUILD and downloading the sources poses no risk of unintended code execution.

As emphasized, missing or skipped checksums would not make this unsafe for this narrow gate — but in this case, valid checksums are present. All operations during `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` are limited to downloading and verifying known-release assets from the project's official repository.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
No dangerous code executed during source fetch</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The provided `.nvchecker.toml` file is a configuration file for nvchecker, a version checking tool commonly used in AUR packages to automate version updates. The configuration defines a single source for the `harharbinks-bin` package, using the GitHub repository `bapatchirag/harharbinks` with the `use_latest_release` option enabled, which instructs nvchecker to track the latest GitHub release tag, prefixed with "v".

This configuration does not contain any executable code, network operations beyond expected GitHub API queries (which are inherent to nvchecker's legitimate use), or file system manipulations. It does not perform or enable any form of arbitrary code execution, data exfiltration, or dynamic fetching of untrusted payloads. The use of `use_latest_release` is standard practice for `-bin` packages that mirror upstream released versions. No obfuscation, suspicious commands, or harmful logic is present.

The file solely serves its intended purpose: declaratively specifying how to track new releases of the associated software. There are no deviations from expected AUR packaging practices.
</details>
